hypotheses.assessment_markdown:
A

### Aaron was American-born; the immigration was earlier.

Moderate working preference

**Why it leads:** the South Carolina record context and Solomon’s later paternal-birthplace statement give affirmative, if qualified, support. This is stronger than reasoning from a missing passenger record.

**What is missing:** a contemporary birth, parentage or childhood record. Earlier residence in America does not establish an American birth.

Most useful test → Direct-Aaron military, land-entry, church or earlier household evidence.
hypotheses.statement: Aaron was American-born; the immigration was earlier.

hypotheses.assessment_markdown:
B

### The deeper paternal family had Irish, possibly Ulster, roots.

Broad direction only

**Why it matters:** relevant A823 comparison labels and the unresolved Devaney match make Ireland a reasonable genetic research direction. Support is low to moderate for the broad direction, low for a specific locality or route.

**What is missing:** independently documented comparison pedigrees and a sufficiently recent paternal connection. Self-reported tester origins and uneven testing cannot locate the immigrant. Scotland remains open.

Most useful test → A younger shared SNP branch paired with independently traced paternal pedigrees.
hypotheses.statement: The deeper paternal family had Irish, possibly Ulster, roots.

hypotheses.assessment_markdown:
C

### A Devaney-related male line eventually used Oliphant.

Low historical confidence

**Why it stays active:** two distinct genetic comparators and documentary or autosomal naming clues make this the leading named family comparison.

**What is missing:** a recent shared paternal branch, a record naming Aaron’s parents, or any documented surname transition. High research priority is not high confidence in the explanation.

Most useful test → Resolve the broad Y67 match and separately compare the A823 tester at mutually readable DNA positions.
hypotheses.statement: A Devaney-related male line eventually used Oliphant.

hypotheses.assessment_markdown:
D

### Aaron connects to the Charleston–Union James and David family.

Low confidence in the link

**Why it stays active:** this is a genuine American Oliphant family with better-documented relationships, land and possible Scottish connections. It broadly fits the remembered tentative James–David suggestion.

**What is missing:** the Aaron bridge. The Union James, dead by January 1793, must remain distinct from a Laurens James alive in October 1797. The painter David and physician David must also remain distinct. The administrator’s identity is still open.

Most useful test → A contemporary record connecting Aaron to that family; the requested Scottish documents may clarify the candidates first.
hypotheses.statement: Aaron connects to the Charleston–Union James and David family.

hypotheses.assessment_markdown:
### The alternative we must keep testing

The Devaney Y connection may be old, while any autosomal Devaney ancestry comes through another branch. An unidentified or untested family may explain the paternal line. Eliminating some named testers cannot prove whichever surname remains.

No positive evidence currently establishes a Jamaica route or places a name change, adoption or mistaken father specifically at Aaron. The lack of an identified birth record is a gap, not proof of any of those events.
hypotheses.statement: The alternative we must keep testing

sections.markdown:
01 / The questions

## Three questions. One unfinished history.

01

### Where did we come from?

Find the family’s home before America, and identify which paternal generation immigrated.

02

### Who came before Aaron?

Identify his parents or earlier family through records that connect people, places and generations.

03

### Why a different paternal line?

Explain the genetic difference from other tested Oliphant branches, including when this line began using the surname.
sections.title: Three questions. One unfinished history.

sections.markdown:
02 / The present answer

## The American story is clearer. The older connection is still missing.

No parent, immigrant generation, overseas home, or surname-transition event has yet been established for Aaron. No single origin theory currently deserves to be called probable.

The strongest progress is a firmer framework for testing those questions. Contemporary records identify Aaron’s wife, stated residences, land transactions and estate. Separately, original court testimony clarifies a proposed James–David Oliphant family. DNA comparisons now distinguish promising unresolved matches from matches whose shared paternal ancestry is much older.

Recorded

### Aaron’s wife and Georgia household have a solid anchor.

A deed dated 29 January 1821 calls Aaron of Hancock County, Georgia, and identifies his wife Rebecca as a daughter of deceased Solomon Rainwater. It names *her* father, not Aaron’s. His estate administration establishes that he was dead by 14 December 1826. [[1]](./index.html#s1) [[4]](./index.html#s4)

Recorded

### The James–David candidate family is more distinct.

George Gordon explicitly acknowledged that he was deceased James Oliphant’s son-in-law. David Oliphant was named as a coadministrator in Charleston. Neither observation identifies Aaron as a relative; David is not thereby proved to be James’s son or the painter. [[6]](./index.html#s6)

Unresolved

### Devaney is a useful comparison, not a recovered former surname.

A relatively close Y67 Devaney match and a separate R-A823 DeVenney tester justify finer comparison. They are two different people, and neither result yet establishes a recent common paternal ancestor with this Oliphant line. [[8]](./index.html#s8)

### The family line we are working from

The reported line through Solomon Rainwater Oliphant to Aaron and Rebecca remains the working family history. The original Bible pages or a complete, sourced transcript have not yet been retrieved. Later accounts may repeat the same source. That is a specific documentation gap, not affirmative evidence of adoption or invented parentage. [[9]](./index.html#s9)
sections.title: The American story is clearer. The older connection is still missing.

sections.markdown:
03 / Aaron in the records

## A life comes into view.

Dates below belong to documents. A purchase does not necessarily establish residence, and people with the same name are not automatically the same person.

- 1809 Candidate only

### An Aaron in Tennessee

An Aaron Oliphant helped prove Thomas Welch’s verbal will in Rutherford County. He has not been identified as Rebecca’s husband. The surviving loose will may preserve useful endorsements absent from the recorded copy. [[10]](./index.html#s10)

- 1814–17 Pendleton, SC

### An estate sale and debt proceedings

An Aaron bought goods at Solomon Rainwater’s December 1814 estate sales. Original registers name Aaron in debt proceedings on 26 December 1816 and 18 March 1817. The family context makes the earlier identity plausible; the sale alone proves neither residence nor kinship. [[2]](./index.html#s2)

- 29 Jan 1821 Hancock, GA

### A marriage relationship stated explicitly

The Pendleton deed identifies Aaron of Hancock County and his wife Rebecca, Solomon Rainwater’s daughter. This is the earliest secure Georgia residence statement found in this investigation. [[1]](./index.html#s1)

- 1823–24 Two distinct tracts

### Land and a more precise district

On 25 December 1823, Aaron of Greene County bought 245¾ acres on Shoulderbone Creek. A separate grant dated 4 March 1824 names Aaron Olliphant of Sharp’s district, Hancock, for 490 acres in original Appling district 1, lot 98. The grant is manuscript page **63**; it does not establish residence on that land. [[3]](./index.html#s3) [[5]](./index.html#s5)

- 1825–26 Greene / Hancock

### A bond, a sale, and an estate

A 1825 bond concerns a different tract of about 230 acres in Hancock. Its Greene residence statement conflicts with the Hancock description in later litigation. Aaron of Hancock sold the 245¾-acre Greene tract on 17 June 1826; the continuation names Rebecca. By 14 December, an administrator had qualified for his estate. [[3]](./index.html#s3) [[4]](./index.html#s4) [[11]](./index.html#s11)

- 1880 A later recollection

### A South Carolina birthplace clue

Solomon’s census entry reports his unnamed father born in South Carolina. The information is late, the informant unidentified, and applying it to Aaron depends on the reported father–son relationship. It supports an American-born working hypothesis without proving Aaron’s birthplace. [[7]](./index.html#s7)
sections.title: A life comes into view.

sections.markdown:
04 / The genetic evidence

## A paternal branch is a clue. It is not an address or a surname.

Y-DNA follows the direct paternal line. Autosomal DNA reflects many ancestral lines. These answer different questions, and a shared surname in an autosomal match’s tree does not identify the source of the shared DNA. [[8]](./index.html#s8)

R-A823

Tested paternal branch

23

Y67 matches reviewed

9

Still too broadly typed for equivalent exclusion

Fourteen of the reviewed Y67 comparators have more-resolved results that place their split on older branches, within the limits described in the private audit. Nine remain insufficiently resolved. This narrows particular comparisons; it cannot exclude every family bearing a surname. [[8]](./index.html#s8)

### Why Devaney stays on the list

One Y67 match is at an official genetic distance of five but is displayed only as broad R-M269. A separate DeVenney tester has R-A823. The needed next step is a finer SNP comparison: do either share a younger branch or reliable private variants with this line?

### Why confidence remains limited

Another five-step Y67 match splits much further back on the paternal tree. Similar STR distance can therefore conceal very different relationships. Shared R-A823, surname spelling counts and reported Irish origins cannot by themselves identify Aaron’s father.

Autosomal comparisons include service-confirmed triangulations, but none has been assigned to Aaron or a unique ancestral couple. Paternal cousins share ancestry through both paternal grandparents. Several surname spellings or related matches may therefore reflect the same connection—or a different branch entirely.

### The missing historical anchor

An independently documented direct-male descendant through another son of Aaron would help test whether this Y line reaches Aaron. A collateral through another son of Solomon would anchor it no earlier than Solomon. A single descendant’s result cannot independently verify every historical father–son link.

This public-facing edition omits living matches’ names, kit identifiers, segment coordinates and account links. The figures above summarize the private comparison reviewed on 29 September 2026. Source and method limits are retained in note 8.
sections.title: A paternal branch is a clue. It is not an address or a surname.

**Question:** where did the debts arise, and do the papers identify residence, associates or genuine handwriting?

**Route:** resolve the ledger-to-loose-series crosswalk with the repository. Candidate custodial series: SCDAH **L53085**, magistrates’ memoranda, file 000001, four folders, **260C04**; **L53095**, Common Pleas papers, 15 microfilm reels; **L53061**, summary petitions/decrees, **AN197/AN198, 1800–1826**. These are not identified Aaron packets. Do not equate Grisham’s summons 1063 with a tested Common Pleas roll 1063 covering 1802–1812. The derivative Lawhon date of 4 December differs from the original register’s 26 December; its procedural meaning is unresolved.

09 · Rutherford County Archives Thomas Welch’s loose will, 1809 Copy read · loose item unread

**Reference:** original loose wills 1804–1899: **Welch, Thomas**, written **14 and 18 May 1809**, recorded **11 July 1809**, RB **1b p82**, nuncupative. Distinguish the later 1842/1843 Welch entry.

**Already read:** recorded will DGS **7642461 images 118–119** and court proof DGS **8142650 image 193, p138**.

**Question and route:** obtain all sides, endorsements and attachments of the listed loose item to test the Tennessee Aaron’s identity. No item scan route or precise box has been found, and no request has been submitted.

10 · Furman University Salem Baptist’s early church register Microfilm identified

**Reference:** Salem Baptist, Anderson County, South Carolina Baptist Historical Collection; church records **1805–1901, 1908–1981**. Start with **1805–1821**. A local guide describes two reels, **A072**; confirm that local designation. [Furman guide](https://libguides.furman.edu/special-collections/sc-baptist-collection/microfilm/church-records).

**Question:** do admissions, dismissals or transfer letters identify Aaron, Rebecca, the Rainwater associates, or an earlier church? An estate notice at Salem Meeting House does not establish membership.

**Route:** confirm relevant surviving contents and microfilm access/loan. No online image route was found in the checked guide; that does not establish that no digitization exists.

11 · SC Department of Archives and History Charleston litigation and surviving alternatives Some originals missing

**1797/5:** Grimké / Oliphant & Gordon, **L10090 box 1**, is catalogued missing. Alternative **L10086 unit 000001** minutes at **138G05–138H01**; exact page unresolved.

**David cases:** **1787/13 Smith; 1787/25 Ballantine; 1788/3 Hamilton**. S142001 units **10** (1787 bundle range still ambiguous), **11** (regular 1788), **22** (oversize, 171K08), **23** (index, 360I02). Alternatives: **S142002 unit 7**, 1785–1790 minutes, 138H08; **S142003 unit 2**, 1784–1790 rough minutes, 138H02; **S142006 unit 1**, 1752–1797 reports, 360I02.

**Chollet case:** [L10018, 1794 roll 0109A, item 000](https://www.archivesindex.sc.gov/index.php/Detail/objects/L1001817940109A000), 26 March 1794. Ask for the full roll and later execution returns; fallback **L10048** executions for the cited 13 June 1801 writ.

**Question:** clarify the candidate James and David’s identities and kinship. None is yet an Aaron bridge. These underlying files remain unread; the recovered Union Tucker case should not be requested again as untouched material.

12 · PRONI / Abercorn Papers Identify the Baronscourt carpenter Location-restricted films

**References:** **D623/A/87/36**, 24 November 1791; **D623/A/87/60**, 30 May 1792; accounts **D623/A/106/1**, 1791–1796. Related A/107/1–2 is a secondary extension. FamilySearch catalogue **452903**; film **1736848 / DGS 8706901** and film **1736910 / DGS 8633284**. Exact images not located.

**Question:** confirm the uncertain surname “Oliphant(?)” and find a forename or earlier employer. The inn-management arrangement was proposed, not recorded as an appointment.

**Route:** authorized center/affiliate film access or PRONI originals. Catalogue transcriptions only have been read. Work at Baronscourt would establish neither Irish birth nor a connection to Aaron.

13 · University of St Andrews Keep the Jamaican Davids distinct Catalogue only

**References:** [ms36220/1727](https://collections.st-andrews.ac.uk/item/letter-james-wedderburn-to-james-paterson-junior-concerning-the-jamaica-estate-of-dr-david-oliphant/2034722), 29 November 1786, letter concerning Dr David Oliphant’s Jamaican estate; [ms36220/1361](https://collections.st-andrews.ac.uk/item/copy-will-of-david-lord-olyphant-dated-16-april-1763-leaving-his-estates-in-jamaica-to-his-wife/2033738), copy of Lord David Olyphant’s 16 April 1763 will, copied about 1770.

**Question:** which relatives and estates belong to each David? Physician, lord and painter must not be blended.

**Route:** manuscript access or copies; no scan was located and no request submitted. These are low-priority identity controls, not current evidence that Aaron came through Jamaica.

14 · Conditional follow-ups Other records that need a sharper target Not order-ready

**Military rolls:** Nash regiment muster, pay and descriptive rolls: NARA **RG 94, PI-17 entries 55A, 55B, 55C; inventory entry 55**, [NAID 654644](https://catalog.archives.gov/id/654644), South Carolina, Lt. Col. Reuben Nash. Unit box, company and individual coverage remain unresolved; originals unread. The South Caroliniana Nash roster typescript, accession **2350**, 18 sheets, OCLC **31399861**, has a catalogue copy marked missing. No Aaron entry has been read in it.

**Bounty land:** NARA **NAID 567388** is a conditional series search, not a located application for Aaron or Rebecca. Resolve soldier identity before ordering an assumed file.

**Scottish goldsmith:** the published 1751 apprenticeship and 1763 burgess entries were read; original Edinburgh manuscript shelfmarks and the American identity bridge remain unresolved.

**Parentage and autosomal assignment:** seek a specifically identified heir, guardian or church record for Aaron’s children; establish the proposed Devaney/Pilcher pedigrees and the actual shared ancestral couple before assigning DNA to that line. No confirmed loose parentage file has yet been identified.

07 / Sources & methods

## A conclusion should lead back to its evidence.

This edition was reconciled against the current claim register and independent reviews of 29 September 2026. It is a synthesis of that work, not a fresh examination of every manuscript. Original-image links may require a free account or access at a participating location; a subscription does not necessarily remove those restrictions.

**Recorded** — the identified record says it; this does not settle every same-name identity.

**Supported inference** — a reasoned connection with a remaining evidentiary gap.

**Unresolved** — the evidence needed to choose among explanations is missing.

Machine text was used to locate records; original readings control the central documentary claims. Copied accounts are not counted as independent witnesses. An unsuccessful search describes only the collections, pages and spellings actually checked. Confidence is qualitative: no surname probabilities have been calculated.

- **Pendleton deed, 29 January 1821.** Book P, p382. Names Aaron of Hancock County and Rebecca as daughter of deceased Solomon Rainwater. [Original image](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSR8-8SHH-B). Original visually read in the research archive; claims A03–A04.

- **Pendleton estate and debt records, 1814–1817.** Solomon Rainwater estate sale, first sale 16 December 1814, saved packet pp11–12; original visually read. [Public scan packet](https://www.therainwatercollection.com/reference/ref1445_solomon-rainwater-estate-sale.pdf), Anderson County Estate Papers, Box 16, #578, Roll C1133; hosted by the Rainwater Collection, source item 1445. Lawhon register, 26 December 1816, [original image](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-N3ZG-16FP); Samuel Taylor register, 18 March 1817, [original image](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-F3ZG-1XL5). Loose writs unread. Claims A01–A02.

- **Greene land purchase and sale.** 25 December 1823, Book JJ pp12–13, recorded 7 January 1825: [purchase image](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSYD-ZQWV-S). 17 June 1826, pp315–317: [sale](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSYD-ZQWW-D) and [continuation](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSYD-ZQW7-7). Original readings; claims A05, A07.

- **Hancock estate administration, 14 December 1826.** Ordinary minutes pp464–465, film 222102, DGS 5761707, image 269. [Original minutes](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QSQ-G935-VV68). Estate accounts Book M pp33–40 and Book N pp185–186 were also examined. These entries do not identify parents or distribute the estate to named children. Claim A08.

- **Appling district 1, lot 98 grant, 4 March 1824.** Georgia Surveyor General, film 511955 item 2, DGS 8657161, image 232, manuscript p63. [Original grant](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-63CH-ZL3K); [O index, image 190](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-D3CH-ZG75). Page 63 corrects an earlier reading of 13. Claim A12. Jurisdiction: [Georgia acts of 1819](https://dlg.usg.edu/record/dlg_zlgl_4361555), act of 14 December, p43; legislative text read, printed image not re-examined for this edition.

- **Tucker equity case, Union bill 10, 1807–1809.** FamilySearch catalogue 476669, film 254981, DGS 8700422. Gordon’s [answer, image 197](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-J38D-H99Q-D) and [oath, image 198](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-J38D-H1WP); David’s Charleston residence in the [bill, image 178](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QHV-J38D-H9MC-4). Original images read. Gordon’s oath is dated 16 January 1809. Claims J03, J05; no Aaron relationship identified.

- **Solomon’s 1880 census.** Lee County, Texas, enumeration district 94, p11/stamped 60, 4 June 1880, dwelling 91/family 92, line 36. [Original image](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33S7-9YBX-9JBP). Independent enlarged reading supports South Carolina in the partly ink-blotted paternal birthplace entry. The unnamed father’s identity and late reporting limit the conclusion. Claim A10.

- **Private genetic observations and independent comparison audit.** Authenticated FamilyTreeDNA and MyHeritage observations, 28–29 September 2026; *DNA Discrimination Independent Audit*, 29 September 2026, reconciled with the Y67 comparison, public-project screen and segment audit. Current claims D01–D07. No recent shared SNP-defined Devaney branch or Aaron-assigned segment has been demonstrated. Private match data are withheld; an appropriately consented technical comparison remains outstanding. The public text alone is not a reproducible release of that dataset.

- **Family Bible provenance and later accounts.** *Bible Parentage Provenance* and *RootsWeb–Oliphant Mirror Audit*, 28 September 2026, current claims P01–P03. A likely January 2002 message-board source groups Solomon with Aaron and Rebecca without an original citation; a [later Rainwater biography](https://www.therainwatercollection.com/gallery/aug2009.shtml) credits the Bible for children’s birthdates. The gallery URL is not proof of when its current wording first appeared. The complete underlying Bible or transcript remains unexamined. This edition does not present those later statements as independent original proof.

- **Thomas Welch will and court proof, Rutherford, 1809.** Recorded will pp82–83, DGS 7642461 images 118–119; minute proof p138, DGS 8142650 image 193. Originals read in the archive. The loose item is listed separately by the county. The Tennessee Aaron’s identity remains unresolved; claims T01–T02.

- **Woodard land bond and later court copy.** Bond dated 26 September 1825, copied in Greene Superior Court proceedings pp112–114, March 1830. [Opening bond](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C3M5-VSP2-W) and [pleading and judgment](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C3M5-VSPJ-J), film 158324, DGS 8458688, images 357–358. Original court copy read; later title comparisons include Hancock DGS 7659219 image 149, pp275–276, and DGS 7659222 image 96, pp143–144. These concern the 230-acre tract, distinct from the 245¾-acre Greene purchase. Claim A06.

- **Interpretation and alternatives.** *Current Claim Register*, *Competing Claims Adversarial Review*, and *Mini Progress Report*, 29 September 2026. Editorial syntheses of the cited record and genetic assessments, not additional historical witnesses. The James/David Scottish identity and Aaron connection remain open (J01–J09); comparative genetic exclusions apply to sampled testers, not entire surnames.

08 / Edition history

## A living report, with a memory.

29 September 2026

### Edition 01 · A consolidated starting point

Reconciles the American chronology, separates the Devaney comparators, preserves the missing Aaron–James/David connection, and brings the outstanding-record agenda into one readable edition.

Corrections carried forward include Appling grant page 63, Gordon’s explicit son-in-law testimony, the separate Davids and Jameses, and the distinction between an accessible marriage register and a bounded search that found no target entry.

Future editions should state which claim changed, what source changed it, and what remains unresolved. Superseded interpretations should remain traceable rather than disappear from the record.

29 September 2026

### Edition 01.1 · A reusable research record

Added generated Markdown and structured JSON, stable hypothesis and retrieval identifiers, and a machine-readable entry point. Reframed the report for any reader. These are presentation and continuity improvements; no new genealogical conclusion follows.

29 September 2026

### Edition 01.2 · Sources and reproducible updates

Added direct estate-packet, biography and court-image links already recorded in the research notes, plus a portable build and continuation guide. No new original-record reading or genealogical conclusion is claimed.

### Use this research in your own work

[Read the full Markdown report](./report.md) · [Structured research (JSON)](./research.json) · [Start here for AI readers](./llms.txt) · [Edition checksums](./manifest.json) · [Research and update guide](./README.md)

These exports contain the same public evidence and qualifications, including expanded retrieval details. They are regenerated together; they do not expose private DNA records. A missing search in this public summary does not mean it has never been attempted.

Editorial note: research assistance includes AI-supported retrieval, synthesis and comparison. Human-readable source references and explicit limits make review possible; they do not turn an inference into a fact. This web edition remains a provisional working report. Original archive images and private DNA materials are not reproduced.
